title: The Board Shows The Work
eyebrow: Three faults you named are fixed, checked and now running; the fourth is a job of its own

actions.fyi: Nothing is waiting on you. The outside round of review has been done and the screen you are looking at is the fixed one. The fourth thing you named — a card never showing its two tags — was living in this job's notes instead of on the board; it is now a job of its own and I start it next unless you say otherwise.

content.label: What you were looking at
content.lead: Four pieces of work were under way and the screen showed none of them.

before.caption: Before — In Progress and In Review both empty

after.caption: After — each job in its own column, showing which step is moving

blocks.label: Your second look was right
blocks.text: The first fix put the claimed steps on screen but left every job sitting in Open, so a job still read as untouched while its own step was being worked. A job now moves with the work under it, at any depth, and its steps stay inside it — one card per job, in the column that is true.

content.label: Why it was empty
content.lead: Two separate reasons, both of which looked like an idle board rather than a fault.

rows.title: Every claimed card was hidden
rows.note: A job is a goal with steps under it, and it is always a step that somebody claims. The screen only drew goals, and a goal stays open until its last step finishes — so however many people were working, the middle columns read zero.

rows.title: Finished work fell back into Open
rows.note: Work that is written but not yet landed has a name the screen did not recognise, so it was filed under Open with a warning marker instead of reaching In Review.

blocks.title: A third one turned up while guarding this
blocks.text: A card you pin to the top of the list had no column either, and would have dropped into Open the same way. It is fixed too, and it was the new check that found it, not me.

content.label: The other two you pointed at
content.lead: The report button was in the wrong place, and the drawers behaved differently.

rows.title: No card seemed to have a report
rows.note: The button existed, but only at the bottom of a card's detail panel, so from the board itself the whole feature read as missing. It is now a strip under the card, and it opens that card's report. Cards without one still show nothing.

rows.title: The two drawers were not the same drawer
rows.note: The report drawer covered more than two thirds of the screen; it now takes under half, and the page lays out its own reading column inside it. The card drawer appeared instantly instead of sliding — it was being built already open, so there was nothing to slide from.

shots.caption: The card drawer caught mid-slide, with the board still readable behind it

content.label: What stops it coming back
content.lead: Both faults now fail loudly instead of quietly reading zero.

items: The work list is asked directly which states it can put a card in, so a state the screen has no column for fails the test suite rather than silently landing in Open.
The rule for which cards reach the columns has its own cases, including the exact shape that caused this: a board where every live card is a step.

A check drives a real browser at the running screen, reads back what each column actually drew, and compares it with the work list card by card. It was switched off twice on purpose — once per fault — and went red both times before being switched back on.

A second check opens each drawer and measures it while it should still be moving, so a drawer that stops sliding, or grows to swallow the screen again, fails instead of merely looking wrong. Each of its two rules was switched off on its own and it named the right drawer each time.

content.label: The outside round of review
content.lead: Read by someone who had not written any of it, once, as you asked.

rows.title: One fault found, and fixed
rows.note: A job that is itself being worked, while one of its steps sits waiting to land, was filed under In Review rather than In Progress — the job's own state was being read as a last resort instead of counting as work like any other. It now counts, and a case that fails without the fix holds it there.

rows.title: Two more filed rather than fixed
rows.note: Searching for a step empties the whole board, because the search matches the step and the screen only draws jobs. And the ring chart on the home page counts by a different rule from the columns beside it, so the two disagree. Both are outside what this job promised, and both are now cards.

blocks.label: The screen you are looking at is the fixed one
blocks.text: The running screen had been left on a build made before the review, so the fix was not actually in front of you. It was rebuilt and restarted, and the card-by-card check was run again against what is now serving: every column agrees with the work list.

decisions.title: A step under way gets its own card; a finished one does not
decisions.why: Work in flight has to be visible wherever it sits, or the columns lie. A finished step belongs inside the goal it finished — listing every one of them again in Closed would bury the goals you actually want to read.

decisions.title: A job is one card, and it moves with the work under it
decisions.why: Overruled by you, and rightly. Drawing the live steps as cards of their own filled the middle columns but left every job in Open and showed each job twice. The job now follows its own work and lists its steps inside itself.

decisions.title: The two drawers are allowed to be different widths
decisions.why: A drawer holding a document and a drawer holding a card's details are not the same thing, and forcing them to match would have made the report unreadable. The rule they both keep is that neither takes more than half the screen.

decisions.title: A card's own state is work like any other
decisions.why: Being worked beats waiting to land wherever either is found, on the card itself or anywhere below it. The alternative — the card's own state only breaking a tie nobody else claimed — is what put a job that was moving into the waiting column.

decisions.title: The tags become their own job rather than a fifth fix here
decisions.why: Showing both tags on a card face and filtering by them is new work with its own before-and-after, not a defect in the column rule. Bolting it on would have left this job with two things to prove and neither one checked.

next.if_nothing: I start the tags job: both tags on every card face, and a filter beside the type filter.
